extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary essays and character sketches; students of 19th-century prose and biographical vignettes
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short literary/biographical sketches that reveal character via anecdote, dialogue, and moralized commentary; often focused vignettes of historical or fictional figures. Emphasis on economy, specificity, and the narrator's voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anecdote to reveal character
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is shown through specific episodes and incidents (e.g., Chevalier's prayer trick, Higden's sudden wins, Andrews' coach bet) rather than abstract description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ decisive, often illustrative anecdotes that crystallize a person's habits, values, or downfall. Include the action, immediate reaction, and consequence; let singular scenes stand for the larger personality. Avoid long lists of traits without illustrative incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialogue (including dialect) to characterize
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct speech, sometimes in dialect or idiosyncratic phrasing (as with Chevalier's prayer), functions as an immediate index of origin, manner, and moral tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give characters distinct voices via quoted speech—phonetic rendering or cadence can signal class, nationality, cunning, or absurdity. Use sparingly and purposefully: dialect must illuminate character and not simply caricature; preserve intelligibility and avoid reducing a person to a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show arc of rise and fall to moralize behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Many sketches trace a gambler's ascent and subsequent ruin (wins followed by losses, imprisonment, death in poverty) to make a moral or social point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure sketches so that gains and losses illustrate consequences of vice or folly. Use the arc to comment on broader themes (e.g., vice, luck, social costs). Avoid anticlimax by ensuring the fall is meaningfully connected to earlier traits or choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratorial irony and evaluative interjection
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator frequently inserts wry remarks, rhetorical questions, or moral judgments (e.g., 'Can there be a greater penalty for unbridled licentiousness?') to frame the anecdote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a consistent narrative voice that can be ironic, moralizing, or amused—use interjections to guide reader interpretation. Balance is key: too heavy-handed moralizing can feel preachy; too detached irony can obscure ethical stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor sketches with vivid, specific detail and locales
rubrics_metrics.description: Precise references—to clubs, streets, sums of money, legal proceedings, and named contemporaries—lend authenticity and situate characters socially and historically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete details (places, institutions, amounts, dated incidents) to ground the sketch and enhance credibility. Use sources (letters, trials, memoirs) when available to add texture. Avoid generic or vague backgrounds that leave the sketch unmoored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodic, vignette-driven structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Each entry concentrates on a short episode or set-piece rather than exhaustive biography (e.g., single duels, single games, one scandalous liaison).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor compact, self-contained scenes that present a telling episode; allow the accumulation of such vignettes to build a portrait. Avoid attempting full-life summaries in the space of a vignette—stick to emblematic moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast and comparison to highlight traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing characters beside each other (e.g., honest winners vs. sharpers, different social ranks) clarifies virtues, vices, and ironies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use juxtaposition—paired anecdotes or tersely sketched foils—to illuminate differences and underline themes. Be careful that contrasts feel purposeful rather than merely name-dropping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contemporaneous documents and named authorities for authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Citing memoirs, letters, trial records, and well-known personalities (e.g., Lord Mansfield, Horace Walpole) is used to corroborate anecdotes and provide social context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolster sketches with references to primary or contemporary sources where appropriate; this lends weight and historicity. When using sources, indicate them succinctly; avoid overloading the sketch with documentary apparatus that interrupts narrative flow.
